idiom_name: Laminar/Airstream: Var state, Signal-derived values, arrows (<--, -->) as bindings
implementation_notes: Laminar wraps Airstream's reactive variables: a Var holds the view-model's state, signals (map/filter) derive view-shaped values, and modifier arrows install the binding - value <-- signal pushes state into a DOM property, onInput --> observer sends events back, giving two-way binding for editors. Elements are built from modifier values, so the 'view' is a Scala expression tree that updates in place instead of re-rendering. Use it for Scala.js front ends; it is the closest Scala equivalent to a binder.
code_sketch:
val user = Var("")
val canSubmit = user.signal.map(_.trim.nonEmpty)
div(
  input(typ := "text", value <-- user.signal, onInput --> user),
  button(
    disabled <-- canSubmit.map(!_),
    onClick --> { _ => submit(user.now()) },
    "Sign in"
  )
)
pitfalls: Subscriptions and Vars need an implicit Owner for lifetimes: creating them outside an owner means they are never cleaned up (or are cut short).
Signals are cold until observed - a derived signal with no observer never runs its computation.
Cross-thread updates (WebSocket callbacks, workers) must be scheduled onto the Airstream owner/transaction, or updates are raced or lost.
Keep Vars private to a component; exposing them lets views write state behind the view-model's back.

variants.name: JavaFX properties used from Scala (ScalaFX)
variants.idiom_name: JavaFX Property/ObservableValue (via ScalaFX wrappers), bindings and FXML
variants.implementation_notes: On the JVM, Scala reaches the same JavaFX property system as Java, usually through ScalaFX's wrappers: a view-model exposes StringProperty-like members, views bind to them (bind / bindBidirectional) and ChangeListener or FXML does the rest. Choose it for JVM desktop apps already using JavaFX; the property primitives and their lazy-evaluation semantics are documented by Oracle and apply unchanged.
pitfalls: bind() makes a property read-only (writes throw); editable controls need bindBidirectional().
ChangeListener registration forces eager evaluation of lazily computed bindings; use invalidation listeners when the value is not needed immediately.
All property access must happen on the JavaFX application thread, and listeners must be removed when a screen closes or views leak.
